name: Build and upgrade equipment
summary: Under approved capital projects the company's own shops rebuild and upgrade its fracturing equipment, most of all converting conventional diesel frac pumps to Tier 4 dynamic gas blending engines with 3,000 HHP continuous duty pumps and idle reduction packages, and building electric versions of sand, blending and chemical units. An equipment engineer turns the fleet design into a work package for each unit, a planner and buyers order engines, transmissions, power ends and kits, and when parts and a shop bay are free the unit is stripped, refabricated, re-engined, rewired and commissioned by heavy-duty technicians, welders, pump and electrical technicians. The unit then passes a commercial vehicle inspection, is signed off by the engineer and released to the fleet, often with a punch list at its first job. Engine and component lead times, bay space while the fleet is busy, and first-of-kind fit problems set the pace.

baseline.org_archetype: A listed Canadian pressure pumper of about 1,350 people, roughly 880 of them field staff on rotation or on call at nine district bases, with a Calgary head office for finance, HR, HSE and engineering.
baseline.notes: Upgrades done in the company's own heavy equipment shops with OEM engine kits; work orders and costs in the ERP maintenance module, drawings and bills of materials in engineering files, commissioning checklists on paper or spreadsheets.

unit_of_work: one unit build or upgrade (for example one frac pump converted to a Tier 4 DGB engine)
trigger: A capital project for a fleet upgrade or new-build programme is approved and the unit is assigned to the shop's build schedule.
end_state: The upgraded or new unit has been commissioned, inspected, recorded as a capital asset and released to an active fleet, with removed engines tagged for sale.

volume.seasonality: Units are pulled into the shop mostly in spring break-up and summer when fleets are idle or light, and less in the winter peak; programme timing follows capital approvals (one fleet of about 14 pumps upgraded every four to six months in 2021-2022).

evidence.note: Three Tier 4 DGB fleets (126,000 HHP) were completed between Q4 2021 and the end of 2022 and a fourth (42,000 HHP) was under way (src4, src12); at 3,000 HHP per pump that is 14 pumps a fleet, about 3 pumps a month, plus electric ancillary units and refurbishments. Agrees with the organisation file's 2-4-8.

surge.cause: Spring break-up shop window, when idle fleets free units for upgrade work

evidence.note: Author's estimate: shops schedule upgrade work into break-up, when most fleets are parked by road bans.
Design packages, technical queries, inspections and release; about 25 hours per unit including a share of fleet design work.

steps.name: Receive approved project and assign the unit
steps.description: The equipment engineer receives the approved capital project, picks the unit numbers to be upgraded in agreement with operations and opens the unit's file with its current configuration and history.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Prepare the unit design package
steps.description: The engineer adapts the fleet design to this unit's trailer and model: layout drawings, engine and transmission mounts, gas train, cooling and electrical changes and the bill of materials, checking weights against axle and permit limits.

error.defect_description: Interference or missing part in the design for this trailer variant

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Approve design and change
steps.description: The director of equipment reviews the package, cost against the capital approval and any change from the fleet design, and approves it under management of change.

control.basis: Management of change for equipment modifications and capital spending authority

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Build work order and parts requisition
steps.description: The maintenance planner creates the work order with operations and labour estimates in the maintenance system and raises requisitions for every item on the bill of materials not in stock.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Place orders for engines and long-lead parts
steps.description: The buyer issues purchase orders to the engine dealer and other suppliers for the DGB engine kit, transmission, continuous duty pump, radiator and controls, confirms promised dates and expedites.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Wait for engines and long-lead parts
steps.description: Engines, transmissions and pumps arrive on suppliers' lead times of several months; in 2021-2022 promised dates slipped and partial shipments were common.

evidence.note: Long lead times on key parts (src4); new builds with Tier 4 engines took about 7-8 months in 2018 (src13). Per-unit waits of one to five months are the author's estimate, since orders are placed for a whole fleet.

steps.name: Receive and stage parts
steps.description: The warehouse attendant receives the engine and parts, checks them against the purchase order and packing list, posts the goods receipt and stages a kit by the bay.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Check kit is complete
steps.description: The planner checks the staged kit against the bill of materials and work order, chases missing items and decides whether the unit can start or must wait.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Wait for a bay and the unit to come off the fleet
steps.description: The shop manager schedules the unit into a bay when one is free and when operations can release the pump from its fleet, usually between pads or during break-up.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Strip the old engine and drivetrain
steps.description: Two heavy-duty technicians lock out the unit, drain fluids, remove the old engine, transmission, radiator and pump with the overhead crane and tag the removed engine and components for resale.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code: lockout of energy sources and safe lifting with overhead cranes

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Fabricate and modify the trailer
steps.description: Welders cut and weld new engine and transmission mounts, the gas train and filtration brackets, guards and walkways, and reinforce the frame where the new layout needs it.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Install engine, transmission and cooling
steps.description: Heavy-duty technicians set the DGB engine, transmission and radiator, align the driveline, and connect fuel, gas, air, exhaust aftertreatment and coolant lines.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Resolve fit problem with engineering
steps.description: The engineer looks at the interference on the shop floor, revises the drawing or approves a field fix, and the welder or technician reworks the part.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Install the pump power end and fluid end
steps.description: Pump technicians mount the continuous duty power end and fluid end, set packing and valves, connect lube and suction and discharge piping, and torque to specification.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Wire controls, gas train and data link
steps.description: Electrical and instrumentation technicians install the engine and pump controllers, gas blending controls, idle reduction package, sensors and the data link to the data van, and test each circuit.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Commission and load test the unit
steps.description: Technicians start the engine, check gas substitution and alarms, and run the pump against a test loop or on the test stand through its rate and pressure range while recording readings on the commissioning checklist.

control.basis: Pressure testing procedure with exclusion zone, and the OEM commissioning procedure for DGB engines

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Troubleshoot and correct faults
steps.description: An electrical technician and the engine dealer's service technician trace the fault (sensor, gas valve, software calibration or leak), correct it and hand the unit back for testing.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Paint, decal and number the unit
steps.description: The welder and fabricator team prepare and paint repaired areas, fit guards, decals and the unit number and pressure ratings plates.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Commercial vehicle inspection of the trailer
steps.description: A licensed heavy-duty technician inspects brakes, lights, suspension, frame and tires to the commercial vehicle inspection standard and issues the inspection certificate and decal.

control.basis: Alberta Commercial Vehicle Inspection Program (CVIP) for heavy trailers

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Engineer inspects and releases the unit
steps.description: The equipment engineer checks the unit against the design, reviews the commissioning and inspection records and the weigh ticket, and signs the release to operations.

control.basis: Engineering release of modified pressure pumping equipment before field use

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Close work order and record the asset
steps.description: The planner closes the work order, records the new engine and pump serial numbers and configuration in the maintenance system and sends the capital cost summary to accounting for capitalisation.

error.defect_description: Serial numbers or costs recorded against the wrong unit

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Hand removed engine to asset disposal
steps.description: The planner lists the removed engine, transmission and pump with condition and hours for the asset disposal team to sell, and moves them to the surplus yard.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Deliver unit to the fleet
steps.description: The unit is hauled from the shop to the district base or the fleet's next pad and joins the fleet's equipment list.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Travel to support the first job
steps.description: A field mechanic drives to the pad where the unit runs its first job to watch start-up and fix early faults.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Clear the first-job punch list
steps.description: The field mechanic tightens leaks, adjusts settings and replaces failed sensors found on the first stages and reports design issues back to the engineer for the next units.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

exceptions.name: Parts short at kit check
exceptions.description: A part promised for the unit has not arrived, so the unit waits again before it can enter a bay.

exceptions.name: Fit problem
exceptions.description: The new engine or mount does not fit this trailer variant and engineering revises the design on the shop floor.

exceptions.name: Commissioning fault
exceptions.description: Testing finds a wiring, gas train or calibration fault and the unit is retested after repair.

exceptions.name: First-job punch list
exceptions.description: A field mechanic supports the unit's first job and clears early faults.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from capital approval to the unit released to a fleet
benchmarks.population: Tier 4 DGB pump upgrades at a Canadian pressure pumper, 2021-2022

evidence.note: A fleet upgrade announced on 12 September 2022 (src12) was expected to be field ready by the end of Q1 2023 (src4), about 200 days for the whole fleet; individual units finish earlier, so the median unit is estimated at about 120 days.
About $32 million for 42,000 HHP (src12), or about $2.3 million per 3,000 HHP pump.

benchmarks.unit: maximum share of diesel replaced by natural gas

pain_points.description: Engine and component lead times are long and promised dates slip, so units wait months and kits arrive incomplete.

evidence.note: Long lead times on key parts (src4); backlogs for transmissions and fluid ends (src13).

pain_points.description: Units can only come into the shop when operations release them, which competes with the winter work season.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

pain_points.description: Trailer variants differ from the fleet design, causing fit problems and rework on the first units of a programme.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of how Canadian oilfield service companies ran this work in 2019-2022.

pain_points.description: Skilled heavy-duty, electrical and pump technicians were scarce in 2021-2022, limiting how many bays could work at once.

evidence.note: Shortage of qualified personnel including technical personnel (src4).

sources.title: Trican Well Service Ltd. Management's Discussion and Analysis for the year ended December 31, 2022
sources.supports: Three Tier 4 DGB fleets (126,000 HHP) operating at end 2022; fourth fleet (42,000 HHP) field ready by end Q1 2023 and fifth approved for early 2024; upgrades include 3,000 HHP continuous duty pumps and idle reduction packages; fully electric sand, blending and chemical equipment developed; capital spending $103.6 million in 2022 mainly Tier 4 upgrades; supply chain challenges such as long lead times on key parts; record inflation; difficulty adding field crews and attracting and retaining qualified personnel; recruiting events; CEWS credited against personnel expenses in 2021 ($10.2 million in cost of sales); the company has safety and training programs; MD&A dated February 22, 2023.

sources.title: Trican Announces Continuation of Low Emissions Fracturing Fleet Upgrade Program
sources.supports: 12 September 2022: fourth set of pumping equipment (42,000 HHP) to be upgraded from conventional diesel to CAT Tier 4 DGB engines for about $32 million, spent in 2022; total Tier 4 capacity 168,000 HHP; DGB displaces up to 85% of diesel; idle reduction technology; 2022 capital budget raised to $114 million.

sources.title: US Onshore Pressure Pumpers Adjusting to New Market Demands
sources.supports: April 2018: lead time for new builds with Tier 4 engines about 7 to 8 months; Tier 4 equipment 10-15% dearer than Tier 2; longer backlogs for transmissions and fluid ends; manufacturers at capacity with refurbishments; refurbishing idle equipment cheaper than buying new.

assumptions: Loaded costs are the organisation file's (base wage x 1.35).
The case modelled is a frac pump conversion to a Tier 4 DGB engine, the most common unit in 2021-2022; electric ancillary builds follow the same steps with more electrical and less engine work.
Engines are ordered for a whole fleet, so the per-unit wait for parts in s06 varies widely; the cycle time median is set mostly by s06 and s09.
Fleet design engineering is spread over the units of a programme; s02 holds only this unit's share and adaptation.

The planner, buyer, warehouse attendant, shop manager, pump technicians, field mechanic and director take part although the process map lists only engineers, welders, heavy-duty and electrical technicians.
The frac pump unit is shown as a resource held out of service during shop work; the organisation file lists only the maintenance shop for this process.

Running costs per hour are left off the maintenance shop and frac pump here: the organisation file's frac pump rate is for pumping (fuel and wear), which a unit in the shop does not incur, and its shop rate is for a whole shop, while one upgrade uses one bay of several.
